content: Worldwide, the majority of individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) acquire the infection either at birth or during early childhood. The clinical course and natural history of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection are highly variable. In some individuals, the infection remains inactive and does not result in significant liver disease. However, in others, it can lead to progressive liver fibrosis, culminating in cirrhosis, end-stage liver disease, and a significantly increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), even in the absence of cirrhosis. These complications typically manifest many years after the initial infection. Longitudinal studies of untreated individuals with CHB indicate a cumulative risk of developing cirrhosis ranging from 8% to 20% over a five-year period. Among those with cirrhosis, there is an approximately 20% annual risk of hepatic decompensation, and the annual incidence of HBV-related HCC is high, varying between less than 1% and 5%. Untreated patients with decompensated cirrhosis have a poor prognosis, with five-year survival rates ranging from 15% to 40%. Several host and viral factors can accelerate disease progression and increase the risk of HCC. These include coinfections with HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), and hepatitis D virus (HDV), as well as other cofactors such as alcohol consumption. Globally, it is estimated that 2 billion people have evidence of past or present HBV infection, and 240 million are chronic carriers of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). The prevalence of HBsAg varies significantly by geographic region, with the highest rates (>5%) observed in sub-Saharan Africa, East Asia, parts of the Balkans, the Pacific Islands, and the Amazon Basin of South America. Nearly half of the global population resides in areas of high HBV endemicity. Updated estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2015 indicated that approximately 650,000 people die annually from complications of CHB. HBV accounts for approximately 45% of HCC cases and 30% of cirrhosis cases worldwide, with much higher proportions in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). HCC is among the top three causes of cancer-related deaths in males, particularly in Southeast Asia. In most regions, the incidence of HCC and cirrhosis is low before the age of 35–40 years but increases exponentially thereafter. However, in certain areas such as Africa, rural western Alaska, and the Amazon, HCC incidence is also high among infected children and young adult males. HBV infection imposes a significant economic burden, particularly in terms of years of life lost due to liver disease, both in high-income settings and LMICs. It is also responsible for 5–10% of liver transplants globally. Many countries have implemented hepatitis B vaccination programs starting at birth or in early childhood. While this strategy has been effective in reducing the incidence and prevalence of HBV in endemic regions over the past few decades, it is unlikely to significantly impact rates of end-stage liver disease or HCC for 20–40 years after the introduction of universal infant immunization. HBV is a small, hepatotropic virus belonging to the Hepadnaviridae family. Liver injury in HBV infection occurs through immune-mediated destruction of infected hepatocytes. HBV is also a recognized oncogenic virus, conferring a higher risk of HCC. The viral genome encodes several proteins, including HBsAg, hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg), the viral polymerase, and the HBx protein. The virus circulates in serum as a 42-nm, double-shelled particle, with an outer envelope containing HBsAg and an inner nucleocapsid containing HBcAg. HBV DNA can be detected in serum and is used to monitor viral replication. Unlike HBsAg and HBcAg, hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) is a soluble protein detectable in serum. At least nine HBV genotypes (A through I) have been identified based on more than 8% genomic sequence divergence. Higher rates of HCC have been observed in individuals infected with genotypes C and F compared to genotypes B or D. Certain subtypes of genotype A, found in southern Africa, are also associated with higher HCC risk, although aflatoxin exposure may contribute to this in sub-Saharan Africa. Antiviral therapy is equally effective across all HBV genotypes, and the HBV vaccine provides protection against all genotypes. Naturally occurring mutations in the pre-core region, which prevent HBeAg synthesis, have been identified in HBeAg-negative individuals with CHB. The functional role of these mutations in liver disease progression remains unclear. HBV is primarily transmitted through percutaneous or mucosal exposure to infected blood and body fluids, including saliva, menstrual, vaginal, and seminal fluids. Sexual transmission is particularly common among unvaccinated men who have sex with men, heterosexual individuals with multiple partners, and those in contact with sex workers. In adults, less than 5% of HBV infections progress to chronic hepatitis. Transmission can also occur through accidental inoculation of small amounts of blood or fluids during medical, surgical, or dental procedures, or through contaminated razors, inadequately sterilized syringes, intravenous drug use, tattooing, body piercing, and acupuncture. Perinatal transmission is a major route of HBV spread in many regions, particularly in China and Southeast Asia, and plays a critical role in maintaining the infection reservoir. Without prophylaxis, a significant proportion of viremic mothers, especially those who are HBeAg-positive, transmit the infection to their infants during or shortly after birth. The risk of perinatal infection is also increased if the mother has acute hepatitis B during the second or third trimester of pregnancy or within two months of delivery. Although in utero transmission is possible, it is uncommon and generally associated with antepartum hemorrhage or placental tears. Horizontal transmission, including household and child-to-child transmission, is also important. In many endemic regions, prior to the introduction of neonatal vaccination, HBV prevalence peaked in children aged 7–14 years.
